AP Statistics · Sampling Distributions · Two Means

Difference of sample means: x̄₁ − x̄₂

第 4 页：先设置两组正态总体的 μ、σ 和 n，再抽 1,000 对。比较偏态时将两组都切至右偏，手动比较 (5, 50) 与 (50, 50)。

Draw a sample from each population, subtract the means, and repeat. Watch the differences pile up into their own distribution — centered at μ₁ − μ₂, with a spread you can predict before you simulate.

Reading it: about 68% of differences should fall within 1 SE of μ₁ − μ₂, about 95% within 2 SE. If the histogram hugs the red curve, the Normal model is doing its job. If both populations are skewed and both n are small, it won't — that's the CLT point.

Try this in class

1 · Shrink the spread

Keep everything else fixed and raise both n from 5 to 50. The center doesn't move — the SE collapses.

2 · Break the Normal shape

Set both populations to Skewed right and both n to 5, then draw 1,000. The difference distribution is visibly non-Normal.

3 · CLT rescue

Same skewed populations, but n = 50 each. The differences turn bell-shaped even though neither population is.

Why variances add: the two samples are independent, so Var(x̄₁ − x̄₂) = Var(x̄₁) + Var(x̄₂) = σ₁2n₁ + σ₂2n₂. Subtracting a random quantity doesn't reduce variability — it adds more. That's why the SE uses + even though the statistic uses −. On their own, σx̄₁ = σ₁n1 and σx̄₂ = σ₂n2.

Empirical vs. Normal model

How to run it: Each “pair” draws n₁ values from Population 1 and n₂ values from Population 2, computes both sample means, and records x̄₁ − x̄₂. Press Space for Draw 1 pair. Changing μ, σ, n, or shape for either population clears the histogram, because the sampling distribution itself has changed. Use Download CSV to save every simulated difference for later analysis.

Assumptions behind the formulas: the two samples are independent, each is a random sample from its population, and each sample is less than 10% of its population (the 10% condition) so the SE formula applies without a finite-population correction.
